{{Short description|Algorithm}}
[[File:Patterns1024Cities2.jpg|thumb|500px|1024 cities that follow exactly [[Zipf's law]], which implies that the first largest city is size 1, the second largest city is size 1/2, the third largest city is size 1/3, ... and the smallest city is size 1/1024. The left pattern is produced by head/tail breaks, while the right one by natural breaks, also known as [[Jenks natural breaks optimization]].]]
'''Head/tail breaks''' is a [[clustering algorithm]] for data with a [[heavy-tailed distribution]] such as [[power laws]] and [[lognormal distribution]]s. The heavy-tailed distribution can be simply referred to the scaling pattern of far more small things than large ones, or alternatively numerous smallest, a very few largest, and some in between the smallest and largest. The classification is done through dividing things into large (or called the head) and small (or called the tail) things around the arithmetic mean or average, and then recursively going on for the division process for the large things or the head until the notion of far more small things than large ones is no longer valid, or with more or less similar things left only.<ref name="Jiang1">{{Cite journal|doi = 10.1080/00330124.2012.700499|title = Head/Tail Breaks: A New Classification Scheme for Data with a Heavy-Tailed Distribution|year = 2013|last1 = Jiang|first1 = Bin|journal = The Professional Geographer|volume = 65|issue = 3|pages = 482–494|arxiv = 1209.2801| bibcode=2013ProfG..65..482J |s2cid = 119297992}}</ref> Head/tail breaks is not just for classification, but also for visualization of big data by keeping the head, since the head is self-similar to the whole. Head/tail breaks can be applied not only to vector data such as points, lines and polygons, but also to raster data like [[digital elevation model]] (DEM).

==Motivation==
The head/tail breaks is motivated by inability of conventional classification methods such as equal intervals, quantiles, geometric progressions, standard deviation, and natural breaks - commonly known as [[Jenks natural breaks optimization]] or [[k-means clustering]] to reveal the underlying scaling or living structure with the inherent hierarchy (or heterogeneity) characterized by the recurring notion of far more small things than large ones.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2016-10-01|title=Calling Dunbar's numbers|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378873316301095|journal=Social Networks|language=en|volume=47|pages=151–155|doi=10.1016/j.socnet.2016.06.003|issn=0378-8733|last1=Mac Carron|first1=P.|last2=Kaski|first2=K.|last3=Dunbar|first3=R.|arxiv=1604.02400|s2cid=14417148}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lux |first1=Marian |last2=Rinderle-Ma |first2=Stefanie |date=2023-01-25 |title=DDCAL: Evenly Distributing Data into Low Variance Clusters Based on Iterative Feature Scaling |journal=Journal of Classification |volume=40 |issue=1 |pages=106–144 |language=en |doi=10.1007/s00357-022-09428-6 |pmid=36713890 |issn=1432-1343 |pmc=9873542}}</ref> Note that the notion of far more small things than large one is not only referred to geometric property, but also to topological and semantic properties. In this connection, the notion should be interpreted as far more unpopular (or less-connected) things than popular (or well-connected) ones, or far more meaningless things than meaningful ones. Head/tail breaks uses the mean or average to dichotomize a dataset into small and large values, rather than to characterize classes by average values, which is unlike k-means clustering or natural breaks. Through the head/tail breaks, a dataset is seen as a living structure with an inherent hierarchy with far more smalls than larges, or recursively perceived as the head of the head of the head and so on. It opens up new avenues of analyzing data from a holistic and organic point of view while considering different types of scales and scaling in [[spatial analysis]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Oshan |first1=Taylor M. |last2=Wolf |first2=Levi J. |last3=Sachdeva |first3=Mehak |last4=Bardin |first4=Sarah |last5=Fotheringham |first5=A. Stewart |date=2022-06-09 |title=A scoping review on the multiplicity of scale in spatial analysis |journal=Journal of Geographical Systems |volume=24 |issue=3 |pages=293–324 |language=en |doi=10.1007/s10109-022-00384-8 |bibcode=2022JGS....24..293O |s2cid=246957819 |issn=1435-5949|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Method==
Given some variable X that demonstrates a heavy-tailed distribution, there are far more small x than large ones. Take the average of all xi, and obtain the first mean m1. Then calculate the second mean for those xi greater than m1, and obtain m2. In the same recursive way, we can get m3 depending on whether the ending condition of no longer far more small x than large ones is met. For simplicity, we assume there are three means, m1, m2, and m3. This classification leads to four classes: [minimum, m1], (m1, m2], (m2, m3], (m3, maximum]. In general, it can be represented as a recursive function as follows:
[[File:HeadTailBreaks Classification Illustration.png|thumb|405x405px|An Illustration of the head/tail breaks classification with 10 numbers]]
     Recursive function '''Head/tail Breaks''':
     Rank the input data values from the biggest to the smallest;
     Compute the mean value of the data
     Break the data (around the mean) into the head and the tail;  
     // the head for data values greater the mean
     // the tail for data values less the mean
     If (length(head)/length(data) <=40%):
         '''Head/tail Breaks'''(head);
     End Function

The resulting number of classes is referred to as ht-index, an alternative index to [[fractal dimension]] for characterizing complexity of fractals or geographic features: the higher the ht-index, the more complex the fractals.<ref name="Jiang2">{{Cite journal|doi = 10.1080/00045608.2013.834239|title = Ht-Index for Quantifying the Fractal or Scaling Structure of Geographic Features|year = 2014|last1 = Jiang|first1 = Bin|last2 = Yin|first2 = Junjun|journal = Annals of the Association of American Geographers|volume = 104|issue = 3|pages = 530–540|arxiv = 1305.0883|s2cid = 62816469}}</ref>

=== Threshold or its sensitivity ===
The criterion to stop the iterative classification process using the head/tail breaks method is that the remaining data (i.e., the head part) are not heavy-tailed, or simply, the head part is no longer a minority (i.e., the proportion of the head part is no longer less than a threshold such as 40%). This threshold is suggested to be 40% by Jiang et al. (2013),<ref name="Jiang3" /> just as the codes above (i.e., (length/head)/length(data) ≤ 40%). This process is called head/tail breaks 1.0. But sometimes a larger threshold, for example 50% or more, can be used, as Jiang and Yin (2014)<ref name="Jiang2" /> noted in another article: "this condition can be relaxed for many geographic features, such as 50 percent or even more". However, all heads' percentage on average must be smaller than 40% (or 41, 42%), indicating far more small things than large ones. Many real-world data cannot be fit into a perfect long tailed distribution, therefore its threshold can be relaxed structurally. In head/tail breaks 2.0 the threshold only applies to the overall heads' percentage.<ref>{{Cite journal|arxiv = 1909.01073|doi = 10.3390/su11154091|title = A Recursive Definition of Goodness of Space for Bridging the Concepts of Space and Place for Sustainability|year = 2019|last1 = Jiang|first1 = Bin|journal = Sustainability|volume = 11|issue = 15|page = 4091|s2cid = 199374168|doi-access = free| bibcode=2019Sust...11.4091J }}</ref> This means that the percentages of all heads related to the tails should be around 40% on average. Individual classes can have any percentage spit around the average, as long as this averages out as a whole. For example, if there is data distributed in such a way that it has a clearly defined head and tail during the first and second iteration (length(head)/(length(data)<20%) but a much less well defined long tailed distribution for the third iteration (60% in the head), head/tail breaks 2.0 allows the iteration to continue into the fourth iteration which can be distributed 30% head - 70% tail again and so on. As long as the overall threshold is not surpassed the head/tail breaks classification holds.

=== Rank-size plot and RA index ===
A good tool to display the scaling pattern, or the heavy-tailed distribution, is the rank-size plot, which is a [[scatter plot]] to display a set of values according to their ranks. With this tool, a new index <ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Gao|first1=Peichao|last2=Liu|first2=Zhao|last3=Tian|first3=Kun|last4=Liu|first4=Gang|date=2016-03-10|title=Characterizing Traffic Conditions from the Perspective of Spatial-Temporal Heterogeneity|journal=ISPRS International Journal of Geo-Information|language=en|volume=5|issue=3|page=34|doi=10.3390/ijgi5030034|bibcode=2016IJGI....5...34G|doi-access=free|hdl=10397/61225|hdl-access=free}}</ref> termed as the ratio of areas (RA) in a rank-size plot was defined to characterize the scaling pattern. The RA index has been successfully used in the estimation of traffic conditions. However, the RA index can only be used as a complementary method to the ht-index, because it is ineffective at capturing the scaling structure of geographic features.

=== Other Indices based on the head/tail breaks ===
In addition to the ht-index, the following indices are also derived with the head/tail breaks.
* CRG-index.  It is developed as a more sensitive ht-index to capture the slight changes of geographic features.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Gao|first1=Peichao|last2=Liu|first2=Zhao|last3=Xie|first3=Meihui|last4=Tian|first4=Kun|last5=Liu|first5=Gang|date=2016-10-01|title=CRG Index: A More Sensitive Ht-Index for Enabling Dynamic Views of Geographic Features|journal=The Professional Geographer|volume=68|issue=4|pages=533–545|doi=10.1080/00330124.2015.1099448|bibcode=2016ProfG..68..533G |s2cid=14967387|issn=0033-0124|hdl=10397/66867|hdl-access=free}}</ref>  In contrast to the ht-index, which is an integer, CRG-index is a real number. 
* Unified metrics. Two unified metrics (UM1 and UM2) were proposed in an AAAG paper <ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Gao|first1=Peichao|last2=Liu|first2=Zhao|last3=Liu|first3=Gang|last4=Zhao|first4=Hongrui|last5=Xie|first5=Xiaoxiao|date=2017-06-02|title=Unified Metrics for Characterizing the Fractal Nature of Geographic Features|journal=Annals of the American Association of Geographers|volume=107|issue=6|pages=1315–1331|doi=10.1080/24694452.2017.1310022|bibcode=2017AAAG..107.1315G |s2cid=134468607|issn=2469-4452}}</ref> for characterizing the fractal nature of geographic features. One can be used to answer the question of "I know there are far more small things than large ones, but how small (or large) are these small (or large) things?", whereas the other one to answer "I know there are far more small things than large ones, but how many more?"
* Fht-index: It is a fractional ht-index, which is able to capture fractional hierarchy.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Jiang|first1=Bin|last2=Ma|first2=Ding|date=2017|title=How complex is a fractal? Head/tail breaks and fractional hierarchy|arxiv= 1703.00814|journal=Journal of Geovisualization and Spatial Analysis|volume=2|pages=xx–xx. Preprint|doi=10.1007/s41651-017-0009-z|s2cid=119466375}}</ref> The fht-index might be of help for creating an intermediate scale between two consecutive map scales, leading to so called continuous map scales.

==Applications==
Instead of more or less similar things, there are far more small things than large ones surrounding us. Given the ubiquity of the scaling pattern, head/tail breaks is found to be of use to statistical mapping, map generalization, cognitive mapping and even perception of beauty
.<ref name="Jiang3">{{Cite journal|arxiv = 1102.1561|doi = 10.1080/00045608.2013.765773|title = Scaling of Geographic Space as a Universal Rule for Map Generalization|year = 2013|last1 = Jiang|first1 = Bin|last2 = Liu|first2 = Xintao|last3 = Jia|first3 = Tao|journal = Annals of the Association of American Geographers|volume = 103|issue = 4|pages = 844–855|s2cid = 119257295}}</ref><ref name="Jiang4">{{Cite journal|doi = 10.1080/00045608.2013.779503|title = The Image of the City out of the Underlying Scaling of City Artifacts or Locations|year = 2013|last1 = Jiang|first1 = Bin|journal = Annals of the Association of American Geographers|volume = 103|issue = 6|pages = 1552–1566|arxiv = 1209.1112|s2cid = 119227287}}</ref><ref name="Jiang5">{{Cite journal|doi = 10.1080/00330124.2013.852037|title = A New Kind of Beauty Out of the Underlying Scaling of Geographic Space|year = 2014|last1 = Jiang|first1 = Bin|last2 = Sui|first2 = Daniel Z.|journal = The Professional Geographer|volume = 66|issue = 4|pages = 676–686|arxiv = 1303.7303| bibcode=2014ProfG..66..676J |s2cid = 119213099}}</ref> It helps visualize big data, since big data are likely to show the scaling property of far more small things than large ones. Essentially geographic phenomena can be scaleful or scale-free. Scaleful phenomena can be explained by conventional mathematical or geographical operations, but scale-free phenomena can not. Head/tail breaks can be used to characterize the scale-free phenomena, which are in the majority.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Chen|first=Yanguang|date=June 2021|title=Characteristic Scales, Scaling, and Geospatial Analysis|url=https://utpjournals.press/doi/10.3138/cart-2020-0001|journal=Cartographica: The International Journal for Geographic Information and Geovisualization|language=en|volume=56|issue=2|pages=91–105|doi=10.3138/cart-2020-0001|arxiv=2001.09819|s2cid=220546091|issn=0317-7173}}</ref> The visualization strategy is to recursively drop out the tail parts until the head parts are clear or visible enough.<ref name="Jiang6">{{Cite journal|doi = 10.1016/j.cities.2014.11.013|title = Head/Tail breaks for visualization of city structure and dynamics|year = 2015|last1 = Jiang|first1 = Bin|journal = Cities|volume = 43|pages = 69–77|arxiv = 1501.03046|s2cid = 119221425}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Wu|first=Jou-Hsuan|url=https://urn.kb.se/resolve?urn=urn:nbn:se:hig:diva-19201|title=Examining the New Kind of Beauty Using the Human Being as a Measuring Instrument|date=2015}}</ref> In addition, it helps delineate cities or natural cities to be more precise from various geographic information such as street networks, social media geolocation data, and nighttime images.

=== Characterizing the imbalance ===
As the head/tail breaks method can be used iteratively to obtain head parts of a data set, this method actually captures the underlying hierarchy of the data set. For example, if we divide the array (19, 8, 7, 6, 2, 1, 1, 1, 0) with the head/tail breaks method, we can get two head parts, i.e., the first head part (19, 8, 7, 6) and the second head part (19). These two head parts as well as the original array form a three-level hierarchy:

* the 1st level (19),
* the 2nd level (19, 8, 7, 6), and
* the 3rd level (19, 8, 7, 6, 2, 1, 1, 1, 0).

The number of levels of the above-mentioned hierarchy is actually a characterization of the imbalance of the example array, and this number of levels has been termed as the ht-index.<ref name="Jiang2" /> With the ht-index, we are able to compare degrees of imbalance of two data sets. For example, the ht-index of the example array (19, 8, 7, 6, 2, 1, 1, 1, 0) is 3, and the ht-index of another array (19, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8) is 2. Therefore, the degree of imbalance of the former array is higher than that of the latter array.
[[File:Natural cities of Germany, created from points of interest.jpg|thumb|250px|right|The left panel pattern contains 50,000 natural cities, which can be put into 7 hierarchical levels. It looks like a hair ball. Instead of showing all the 7 hierarchical levels, we show 4 top levels, by dropping out 3 low levels. Now with the right panel, the scaling pattern of far more small cities than large ones emerges. The right pattern (or the remaining part after dropping out the tails) is self-similar to the whole (or the left pattern). Thus the right pattern reflects the underlying structure of the left one, and enables us to see the whole.]]
[[File:Headtail breaks of American DEM.jpg|thumb|250px|The scaling pattern of US terrain surface is distorted by the natural breaks, but revealed by the head/tail breaks.]]

=== Delineating natural cities ===
The use of fractals in modelling human geography has for a longer period been seen as useful in measuring the spatial distribution of human settlements.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Tannier |first=Cécile |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/book/10.1002/9781394306565 |title=Fractal Geometry in Human Geography and Planning |date=2024-08-27 |publisher=Wiley |isbn=978-1-78945-159-7 |edition=1 |language=en |doi=10.1002/9781394306565.ch2}}</ref> Head/tail breaks can be used to do just that with a concept called natural cities. The term 'natural cities' refers to the human settlements or human activities in general on Earth's surface that are naturally or objectively defined and delineated from massive geographic information based on head/tail division rule, a non-recursive form of head/tail breaks.<ref name="Jiang7">{{Cite journal|doi = 10.1080/00330124.2014.968886|title = The Evolution of Natural Cities from the Perspective of Location-Based Social Media|year = 2015|last1 = Jiang|first1 = Bin|last2 = Miao|first2 = Yufan|journal = The Professional Geographer|volume = 67|issue = 2|pages = 295–306|arxiv = 1401.6756| bibcode=2015ProfG..67..295J |s2cid = 119191062}}</ref><ref name="Long">{{Cite journal|doi = 10.1016/j.apgeog.2016.08.002|title = Redefining Chinese city system with emerging new data|year = 2016|last1 = Long|first1 = Ying|journal = Applied Geography|volume = 75|pages = 36–48| bibcode=2016AppGe..75...36L }}</ref> Such geographic information could be from various sources, such as massive street junctions<ref name="Long"/> and street ends, a massive number of street blocks, nighttime imagery and social media users' locations etc. Based on these the different urban forms and configurations detected in cities can be derived.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Song|first1=Yongze|last2=Long|first2=Ying|last3=Wu|first3=Peng|last4=Wang|first4=Xiangyu|date=2018-12-02|title=Are all cities with similar urban form or not? Redefining cities with ubiquitous points of interest and evaluating them with indicators at city and block levels in China|journal=International Journal of Geographical Information Science|volume=32|issue=12|pages=2447–2476|doi=10.1080/13658816.2018.1511793|bibcode=2018IJGIS..32.2447S |s2cid=52926942|issn=1365-8816}}</ref> Distinctive from conventional cities, the adjective 'natural' could be explained not only by the sources of natural cities, but also by the approach to derive them [http://www.tu1305.eu/sites/default/files/Jingya%20-%20NTL_COST.pdf]. Natural cities are derived from a meaningful cutoff averaged from a massive number of units extracted from geographic information.<ref name="Jiang6"/> Those units vary according to different kinds of geographic information, for example the units could be area units for the street blocks and pixel values for the nighttime images.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2021-08-01|title=Using nighttime light data to identify the structure of polycentric cities and evaluate urban centers|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0048969721016545|journal=Science of the Total Environment|language=en|volume=780|article-number=146586|doi=10.1016/j.scitotenv.2021.146586|issn=0048-9697|last1=Yang|first1=Zhiwei|last2=Chen|first2=Yingbiao|last3=Guo|first3=Guanhua|last4=Zheng|first4=Zihao|last5=Wu|first5=Zhifeng|pmid=33765471|bibcode=2021ScTEn.78046586Y|s2cid=232366838|url-access=subscription}}</ref> A '''[https://www.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=47b1d6fdd1984a6fae916af389cdc57d natural cities model]''' has been created using [[ArcGIS]] model builder,<ref name="Ren">Ren, Zheng (2016). "Natural cities model in ArcGIS", https://www.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=47b1d6fdd1984a6fae916af389cdc57d.</ref> it follows the same process of deriving natural cities from location-based social media,<ref name="Jiang7"/> namely, building up huge triangular irregular network (TIN) based on the point features (street nodes in this case) and regarding the triangles which are smaller than a mean value as the natural cities. These natural cities can also be created from other open access information like [[OpenStreetMap]] and further be used as an alternative delineation of administrative boundaries.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Xiao |first1=Zhiyang |last2=Peng |first2=Zhenhan  |last3=Yu |first3=Zidong |last4=Liu |first4= Xintao |title=Generating Natural Cities Using 3D Road Network to Explore Living Structure: A Case Study in Hong Kong |journal=Smart Cities |date=2023 |volume=6 |issue=3 |pages=1485–1506 |doi=10.3390/smartcities6030070 |issn=2624-6511 |doi-access=free |hdl=10397/108699 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> [[Power law|Scaling law]] can also at the same time correctly be identified and the administrative borders can be created to respect this by the delineation of the natural cities.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Alvioli|first=Massimiliano|date=2020|chapter=Comparative study of delineation of urban areas using imperviousness products and open data|journal=<!-- -->|volume=1|pages=1–4|doi=10.30437/GEOMORPHOMETRY2020_1 |editor1=Massimiliano Alvioli |editor2=Ivan Marchesini |editor3=Laura Melelli |editor4=Peter Guth |title=Proceedings of the Geomorphometry 2020 Conference|publisher=IRPI CNR}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Alvioli|first=Massimiliano|date=2020-12-01|title=Administrative boundaries and urban areas in Italy: A perspective from scaling laws|journal=Landscape and Urban Planning|language=en|volume=204|article-number=103906|doi=10.1016/j.landurbplan.2020.103906|pmid=32834266|pmc=7424309|bibcode=2020LUrbP.20403906A |issn=0169-2046}}</ref> This type methodology can help urban geographers and planners by correctly identifying the effective urban territorial scope of the areas they work in.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kong|first1=Liang|last2=He|first2=Zhengwei|last3=Chen|first3=Zhongsheng|last4=Luo|first4=Mingliang|last5=Du|first5=Zhong|last6=Zhu|first6=Fuquan|last7=He|first7=Li|date=April 2021|title=Spatial Distribution and Morphological Identification of Regional Urban Settlements Based on Road Intersections|journal=ISPRS International Journal of Geo-Information|language=en|volume=10|issue=4|page=201|doi=10.3390/ijgi10040201|bibcode=2021IJGI...10..201K|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Natural cities can vary depending on the scale on which the natural cities are delineated, which is why optimally they have to be based on data from the whole world. Due to that being computationally impossible, a country or county scale is suggested as alternative.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Montero|first1=Gaëtan|last2=Tannier|first2=Cécile|last3=Thomas|first3=Isabelle|date=2021-01-12|title=Delineation of cities based on scaling properties of urban patterns: a comparison of three methods|journal=International Journal of Geographical Information Science|volume=35|issue=5|pages=919–947|doi=10.1080/13658816.2020.1817462|bibcode=2021IJGIS..35..919M |s2cid=233302662|issn=1365-8816|url=https://hal.science/hal-03113934 |hdl=2078.1/254040|hdl-access=free}}</ref> Due to the scale-free nature of natural cities and the data they are based on there are also possibilities to use the natural cities method for further measurements. One of the main advantages of natural cities is that it is derived [[Top-down and bottom-up design|bottom-up]] instead of [[Top-down and bottom-up design|top-down]]. That means that the borders are determined by the data of something physical rather than determined by an administrative government or administration.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2019-09-01|title=A bottom-up approach for delineating urban areas minimizing the connection cost of built clusters: Comparison with top-down-based densely inhabited districts|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0198971518305039|journal=Computers, Environment and Urban Systems|language=en|volume=77|article-number=101363|doi=10.1016/j.compenvurbsys.2019.101363|issn=0198-9715|last1=Usui|first1=Hiroyuki|bibcode=2019CEUS...7701363U |s2cid=199101138|url-access=subscription}}</ref> For example by calculating the natural cities of a natural city recursively the dense areas within a natural city are identified. These can be seen as city centers for example. By using the natural cities method in this way further border delineations can be made dependent on the scale the natural cities were generated from.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=de Rijke|first1=Chris A.|last2=Macassa|first2=Gloria|last3=Sandberg|first3=Mats|last4=Jiang|first4=Bin|date=November 2020|title=Living Structure as an Empirical Measurement of City Morphology|journal=ISPRS International Journal of Geo-Information|language=en|volume=9|issue=11|page=677|doi=10.3390/ijgi9110677|bibcode=2020IJGI....9..677D|doi-access=free}}</ref> Natural cities derived from smaller regional areas will provide less accurate but still usable results in certain analysis, like for example determining urban expansion over time.<ref name="ReferenceA">{{Cite journal|date=2021-07-01|title=How urban expansion affects the thermal environment? A study of the impact of natural cities on the thermal field value and footprint of thermal environment|journal=Ecological Indicators|language=en|volume=126|article-number=107632|doi=10.1016/j.ecolind.2021.107632|issn=1470-160X|doi-access=free|last1=Yang|first1=Zhiwei|last2=Chen|first2=Yingbiao|last3=Wu|first3=Zhifeng|bibcode=2021EcInd.12607632Y }}</ref> As mentioned before though, optimally natural cities should be based on a massive amount of for example street intersections for an entire country or even the world. This is because natural cities are based on [[The Wisdom of Crowds|the wisdom of crowds]] thinking, which needs the biggest set of available data for the best results. Also note that the structure of natural cities can be considered to be [[fractal]] in nature.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Zhang|first1=Hong|last2=Lan|first2=Tian|last3=Li|first3=Zhilin|date=2021-09-08|title=Fractal evolution of urban street networks in form and structure: a case study of Hong Kong|journal=International Journal of Geographical Information Science|volume=36 |issue=6 |pages=1100–1118|doi=10.1080/13658816.2021.1974451|s2cid=239633141|issn=1365-8816}}</ref>

It is important when head/tail breaks are being used to generate natural cities, that the data is not aggregated afterwards. For example, the amount of generated natural cities can only be known after they are generated. It is not possible to use a pre-defined number of cities for an area or country and aggregate the results of the natural cities to administratively determined city borders. Naturally natural cities should follow [[Zipf's law]], if they do not, the area is most likely too small, or data has probably been processed wrongly. An example of this is seen in a research where head/tail breaks were used to extract natural cities, but they were aggregated to administrative borders, which following that concluded that the cities do not follow [[Zipf's law]].<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2021-07-01|title=Did Zipf's Law hold for Chinese cities and why? Evidence from multi-source data|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0264837721001836|journal=Land Use Policy|language=en|volume=106|article-number=105460|doi=10.1016/j.landusepol.2021.105460|issn=0264-8377|last1=Sun|first1=Xiangdong|last2=Yuan|first2=Ouyang|last3=Xu|first3=Zhao|last4=Yin|first4=Yanhui|last5=Liu|first5=Qian|last6=Wu|first6=Ling|bibcode=2021LUPol.10605460S |s2cid=235513633|url-access=subscription}}</ref> This happens more often in science, where papers actually produce results which are actually false.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Ioannidis|first=John P. A.|date=2005-08-30|title=Why Most Published Research Findings Are False|journal=PLOS Medicine|language=en|volume=2|issue=8|article-number=e124|doi=10.1371/journal.pmed.0020124|issn=1549-1676|pmc=1182327|pmid=16060722 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

=== Color rendering DEM ===
[[File:GoldenRationRectangles.png|thumb|The spiral layout illustrates eight levels of hierarchy derived from a fictitious dataset of 5,000 cities, whose sizes follow a rank-size distribution. Cities are represented by points using a spectrum colormap, ranging from red (largest) to blue (smallest).
]]
Current color renderings for DEM or density map are essentially based on conventional classifications such as natural breaks or equal intervals, so they disproportionately exaggerate high elevations or high densities. As a matter of fact, there are not so many high elevations or high-density locations.<ref name="Jiang8">{{Cite journal|jstor = 24432599|last1 = Jiang|first1 = Bin|title = Geospatial analysis requires a different way of thinking: The problem of spatial heterogeneity|journal = GeoJournal|year = 2015|volume = 80|issue = 1|pages = 1–13|doi = 10.1007/s10708-014-9537-y|arxiv = 1401.5889| bibcode=2015GeoJo..80....1J |s2cid = 119248806}}</ref> It was found that coloring based head/tail breaks is more favorable than those by other classifications.<ref name="Wu">Wu, Jou-Hsuan (2015). "Examining the new kind of beauty using the human being as a measuring instrument", http://www.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:805296/FULLTEXT01.pdf.</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Lin|first=Yue|url=https://urn.kb.se/resolve?urn=urn:nbn:se:hig:diva-15609|title=A Comparison Study on Natural and Head/tail Breaks Involving Digital Elevation Models|date=2013}}</ref> [https://ibis.health.state.nm.us/resource/MapChoroClasses.html]

=== Mapping scaling hierarchy ===
The pattern of far more small things than large ones frequently recurs in geographical data. A spiral layout inspired by the [[golden ratio]] or Fibonacci sequence can help visualize this recursive notion of scaling hierarchy and the different levels of scale.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1 = Jiang|first1 = Bin|title = The fractal nature of maps and mapping|journal = International Journal of Geographical Information Science|year = 2015|volume = 29|issue = 1|pages = 159–174|doi = 10.1080/13658816.2014.953165|arxiv = 1406.5410| bibcode=2015IJGIS..29..159J }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1 = Jiang|first1 = Bin|last2 = de Rijke|first2 = Chris|title = Representing geographic space as a hierarchy of recursively defined subspaces for computing the degree of order|journal = Computers, Environment and Urban Systems|year = 2022|volume = 92|article-number = 101750|doi = 10.1016/j.compenvurbsys.2021.101750|arxiv = 2201.08211| bibcode=2022CEUS...9201750J }}</ref> In other words, from the smallest to the largest scale, a map can be seen as a map of a map of a map, and so on.

=== Further applications ===
Other applications of Head/tail breaks:

* Serving as a method for efficiently estimating the absolute [[Boltzmann's entropy formula|Boltzmann's entropy]] of numerical raster data<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Zhang|first1=Hong|last2=Wu|first2=Zhiwei|date=February 2020|title=A Head/Tail Breaks-Based Method for Efficiently Estimating the Absolute Boltzmann Entropy of Numerical Raster Data|journal=ISPRS International Journal of Geo-Information|language=en|volume=9|issue=2|page=103|doi=10.3390/ijgi9020103|bibcode=2020IJGI....9..103Z|doi-access=free}}</ref>
* Quantifying the multiscale representation of a polyline<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Liu|first1=Pengcheng|last2=Xiao|first2=Tianyuan|last3=Xiao|first3=Jia|last4=Ai|first4=Tinghua|date=2020-04-22|title=A multi-scale representation model of polyline based on head/tail breaks|journal=International Journal of Geographical Information Science|volume=34|issue=11|pages=2275–2295|doi=10.1080/13658816.2020.1753203|bibcode=2020IJGIS..34.2275L |s2cid=219075004|issn=1365-8816}}</ref>
* Increasing computational efficiency in [[data-flow analysis]] by emphasizing the head part of the flow dataset<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Tao|first1=Ran|last2=Gong|first2=Zhaoya|last3=Ma|first3=Qiwei|last4=Thill|first4=Jean-Claude|date=May 2020|title=Boosting Computational Effectiveness in Big Spatial Flow Data Analysis with Intelligent Data Reduction|journal=ISPRS International Journal of Geo-Information|language=en|volume=9|issue=5|page=299|doi=10.3390/ijgi9050299|bibcode=2020IJGI....9..299T|doi-access=free}}</ref>
* Temporal analysis of urban expansion related to the [[Urban heat island|thermal environment]]<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Yang|first1=Zhiwei|last2=Chen|first2=Yingbiao|last3=Wu|first3=Zhifeng|last4=Qian|first4=Qinglan|last5=Zheng|first5=Zihao|last6=Huang|first6=Qingyao|date=2019-09-01|title=Spatial heterogeneity of the thermal environment based on the urban expansion of natural cities using open data in Guangzhou, China|journal=Ecological Indicators|language=en|volume=104|pages=524–534|doi=10.1016/j.ecolind.2019.05.032|bibcode=2019EcInd.104..524Y |s2cid=182075528|issn=1470-160X}}</ref>
* Image analysis where [[anisotropy]] is measured in point patterns extracted with a digital pulse transform with the use of head/tail breaks<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Fabris-Rotelli|first1=I.|last2=Stein|first2=A.|date=2020-05-26|title=Use of fractals to measure anisotropy in point patterns extracted with the DPT of an image|journal=Spatial Statistics|volume=42|language=en|article-number=100452|doi=10.1016/j.spasta.2020.100452|s2cid=219785078|issn=2211-6753|url=https://research.utwente.nl/en/publications/use-of-fractals-to-measure-anisotropy-in-point-patterns-extracted-with-the-dpt-of-an-image(f102b884-19ab-47e9-af0c-f35e7059b37b).html}}</ref>
* Visualizing and analyzing spatial patterns in [[bilateral trade]]<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ye|first1=Sijing|last2=Song|first2=Changqing|last3=Cheng|first3=Changxiu|last4=Shen|first4=Shi|last5=Gao|first5=Peichao|last6=Zhang|first6=Ting|last7=Chen|first7=Xiaoqiang|last8=Wang|first8=Yuanhui|last9=Wan|first9=Changjun|date=June 2020|title=Digital Trade Feature Map: A New Method for Visualization and Analysis of Spatial Patterns in Bilateral Trade|journal=ISPRS International Journal of Geo-Information|language=en|volume=9|issue=6|page=363|doi=10.3390/ijgi9060363|bibcode=2020IJGI....9..363Y|doi-access=free}}</ref>
* To identify urban function graphs,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chen|first1=Yimin|last2=Chen|first2=Xinyue|last3=Liu|first3=Zihui|last4=Li|first4=Xia|date=2020-02-01|title=Understanding the spatial organization of urban functions based on co-location patterns mining: A comparative analysis for 25 Chinese cities|journal=Cities|language=en|volume=97|article-number=102563|doi=10.1016/j.cities.2019.102563|s2cid=214502259|issn=0264-2751}}</ref> note that this paper applies head/tail breaks on a [[Normal distribution|Gaussian]] [[kernel density estimation]] which reduces the accuracy of the head/tail breaks method. Essentially a natural cities approach is taken but the initial data chosen to perform head/tail breaks on has been reduced beforehand. For a better representation of urban function graphs head/tail breaks may be applied as the first step in delineating these areas.
* Analyzing structures or hotspots naturally occurring within data to highlight areas of interest (Based on natural cities).

For example within [[biodiversity]] and [[pedodiversity]] studies where there seem to be fractal relationships such as [[Species–area relationship|taxa-area relationships]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ibáñez|first1=J. J.|last2=Ramírez-Rosario|first2=B.|last3=Fernández-Pozo|first3=L. F.|last4=Brevik|first4=E. This can be identified and highlighted by using head/tail breaks.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ibáñez|first1=J. J.|last2=Ramírez-Rosario|first2=B.|last3=Fernández-Pozo|first3=L. F.|last4=Brevik|first4=E. C.|title=Land System Diversity, Scaling Laws, and Polygons Map Analysis|journal=European Journal of Soil Science|year=2020|volume=72|issue=2|language=en|pages=656–666|doi=10.1111/ejss.13035|s2cid=225482696|issn=1365-2389|hdl=10662/23912|hdl-access=free}}</ref>
* In [[Image texture|image feature and texture]] extraction, certain algorithms like the discrete pulse transform, where [[Lulu smoothing|LULU smoothing]] is used to extract the features, can be sped up by using head/tail breaks in the algorithm by separating large features and smaller features more effectively.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lancey|first1=Mark de|last2=Fabris-Rotelli|first2=Inger|date=2020-12-08|title=Ht-index for empirical evaluation of the sampled graph-based Discrete Pulse Transform|journal=South African Computer Journal|language=en|volume=32|issue=2|doi=10.18489/sacj.v32i2.849|issn=2313-7835|doi-access=free|hdl=2263/81190|hdl-access=free}}</ref>
* By analysing hierarchies in urban patterns (i.e. Streets, building outlines), visual salience can be determined because it follows a similar principle, namely a scaling law, or long tailed distribution. Head/tail breaks are an aid in determining the hierarchies present because of the scaling nature of urban morphology and could be of further use when studying urban street network applications.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2020-03-01|title=Capturing what human eyes perceive: A visual hierarchy generation approach to emulating saliency-based visual attention for grid-like urban street networks|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0198971519303072|journal=Computers, Environment and Urban Kwan|last3=Kwan|first3=Mei-Po|last4=Zuo|first4=Zejun|last5=Wan|first5=Bo|last6=Zhou|first6=Shunping|last7=Li|first7=Shengwen|last8=Ye|first8=Yaqin|last9=Qian|first9=Haoyue|last10=Pan|first10=Xiaofang|bibcode=2020CEUS...8001454Z |s2cid=211830143|url-access=subscription}}</ref> This is especially the case for accessibility analysis, combined with [[space syntax]] head/tail breaks allow for an in depth understanding of street |first2=Mebirouk |last3=Abdelkader |first3=Djedid |date=2023-08-25 |title=Exploring Urban Coherence through Fractality, Connectivity, and Arteriality of the Urban Street Network: Comparative Study of Five Medium-Sized Algerian Cities|journal=Journal of Urban Planning and Development |language=en |volume=149 |issue=4|doi=10.1061/JUPDDM.UPENG-4438  |issn=1943-5444}}</ref>
* Urban structures, like street networks have been proven to be fractal in nature. This structure is not consisting of only one defined fractal, it is characterized by a multifractal [[complex network]]. This means that on different scales, the defined fractal can change. Head/tail breaks can be used to determine the structure of the complex network over different scales, as it adjusts based on the data with each new hierarchy.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Long|first1=Yuqing|last2=Chen|first2=Yanguang|date=2021-02-18|title=Multifractal scaling analyses of urban street network structure: The cases of twelve megacities in China|journal=PLOS ONE|language=en|volume=16|issue=2|article-number=e0246925|doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0246925|issn=1932-6203|pmc=7891711|pmid=33600472|arxiv=2004.05545|bibcode=2021PLoSO..1646925L|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Tripathy|first1=Pratyush|last2=Rao|first2=Pooja|last3=Balakrishnan|first3=Krishnachandran|last4=Malladi|first4=Teja|date=2020-11-02|title=An open-source tool to extract natural continuity and hierarchy of urban street networks|journal=Environment and Planning B: Urban Analytics and City Science|volume=48|issue=8|language=en|pages=2188–2205|doi=10.1177/2399808320967680|s2cid=228836992|issn=2399-8083}}</ref>
* Head/tail breaks as a classification method can be used to visualize growth or spread patterns in for example a global pandemic, like the Covid-19 one. By using head/tail breaks, main spread events can be effectively mapped and visualized where locations with a high infection rate are highlighted specifically due to them being in the highest class.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Jiang|first1=Bin|last2=de Rijke|first2=Chris|date=2021-02-08|title=A power-law-based approach to mapping COVID-19 cases in the United States|journal=Geo-spatial Information Science|volume=24|issue=3|pages=333–339|doi=10.1080/10095020.2020.1871306|bibcode=2021GSIS...24..333J |issn=1009-5020|doi-access=free}}</ref> The risk measurement model based on the head/tail breaks approach can describe the spatial and temporal evolution characteristics of the risk of COVID-19, and can better predict the risk trend of future epidemics in each city and identify the risk of future epidemics even during low incidence periods.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Tingting|first1=Wu|last2=Bisong|first2=Hu|last3=Jin|first3=Luo|last4=Shuahua|first4=Qi|date=2023-11-29|title=A Head/Tail Breaks-Based Approach to Characterizing Space-Time Risks of COVID-19 Epidemic in China's Cities|journal=ISPRS International Journal of Geo-Information |volume=12|issue=12|page=485|doi=10.3390/ijgi12120485|issn=2220-9964|doi-access=free|bibcode=2023IJGI...12..485W }}</ref> 
* Rock fracture networks are properties of rocks which are very important in rock engineering with applications in mining, shale gas development or slope stability. Because of the [[self-similarity]] characteristics of these fractures combined with the [[fractal]] nature they inhibit, head/tail breaks provide accurate measurements and analysis into these rock fracture networks.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2019-12-01|title=The fractal description model of rock fracture networks characterization|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0960077919303078|journal=Chaos, Solitons & Fractals|language=en|volume=129|pages=71–76|doi=10.1016/j.chaos.2019.07.055|issn=0960-0779|last1=Sui|first1=Lili|last2=Yu|first2=Jian|last3=Cang|first3=Dingbang|last4=Miao|first4=Wenjing|last5=Wang|first5=Heyuan|last6=Zhang|first6=Jiwei|last7=Yin|first7=Shuaifeng|last8=Chang|first8=Keliang|bibcode=2019CSF...129...71S|s2cid=203042762|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sui |first1=Lili |last2=Wang |first2=Heyuan |last3=Wu |first3=Jinsui |last4=Zhang |first4=Jiwei |last5=Yu |first5=Jian |last6=Ma |first6=Xinyu |last7=Sun |first7=Qiji |date=July 2022 |title=Fractal Description of Rock Fracture Networks Based on the Space Syntax Metric |journal=Fractal and Fractional |language=en |volume=6 |issue=7 |page=353 |doi=10.3390/fractalfract6070353 |issn=2504-3110|doi-access=free }}</ref>
* Classifying tourist attractions into most visited, least visited and something in between for further research into the optimal route of sightseeing busses.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yuo |first1=Tony Shun-Te |last2=Chen |first2=Wei Vicky |last3=Tseng |first3=Tzuhui Angie |date=2022-11-26 |title=Optimizing the routes of the hop-on hop-off sightseeing bus in Taipei city: a new method based on the criteria from major tourism cities |journal=Current Issues in Tourism |volume=26 |issue=21 |pages=3422–3438 |doi=10.1080/13683500.2022.2142096 |s2cid=254034731 |issn=1368-3500}}</ref>
* Measuring the heterogeneity of crime distribution quantitatively while simultaneously considering the statistical and geometrical characteristics of crime distribution.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=He |first1=Zhanjun |last2=Wang |first2=Zhipeng |last3=Gu |first3=Yu |last4=An |first4=Xiaoya |date=2023-10-23 |title=Measuring the Influence of Multiscale Geographic Space on the Heterogeneity of Crime Distribution |journal=ISPRS International Journal of Geo-Information |language=en |volume=12 |issue=10 |page=353 |doi=10.3390/ijgi12100437 |bibcode=2023IJGI...12..437H |issn=2220-9964 |doi-access=free }}</ref>
* Examining the urban sustainability of socioeconomic and environmental dynamics. The natural cities serve as the basic urban form measures to objectively capture the spatial patterns of the sustainability change.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Loo |first1=Becky P.Y. |last2=Tsoi |first2=K.H. |last3=Feng |first3=X. |last4=Zhang |first4=H.|last5=Lin |first5=Y.|last6=Huang |first6=Z.|last7=Lafortezza |first7=R.|last8=Xu |first8=Z.|last9=Lin |first9=H.|date=2024-04-01 |title=Cities and Urbanization: Balancing the Environmental and Socioeconomic Dimensions of Sustainability |journal=Advanced Sustainable Systems |language=en |volume=12 |issue=10 |page=353 |doi=10.1002/adsu.202300401 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2024AdSSy...800401L |hdl=11586/470087 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

== Software implementation ==
The following implementations are available under [[Free and open-source software|Free/Open Source Software]] licenses.
* '''[https://github.com/digmaa/HeadTailBreaks HT calculator]''': a winform application for obtaining related metrics of head/tail breaks applying on a single data array.
* '''[http://jsfiddle.net/mhkeller/5yATK/ HT in JavaScript]''': a JavaScript implementation for applying head/tail breaks on a single data array.
* '''[http://fromto.hig.se/~bjg/axwoman/ HT Mapping tool]''': a function in the free plug-in Axwoman 6.3 to [[ArcMap]] 10.2 that conducts geo-data symbolization automatically based on the head/tail breaks classification.
* '''[https://github.com/chad-m/head_tail_breaks_algorithm HT in Python]''': Python and JavaScript code for the head/tail breaks algorithm. It works great for choropleth map coloring.
* '''[[PySAL]]''': Python classification schemes for choropleth mapping, including head/tail breaks map classification.
* '''[http://pypi.python.org/pypi/smoomapy smoomapy 0.1.9]''': Brings smoothed maps through python.
* [https://doi.org/10.13140/RG.2.1.3041.0324 Ht-index calculator]: A PostgreSQL function for calculating ht-index (also see <ref>{{Cite book|title=A PostgreSQL function for calculating the ht-index |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/287533541 |doi=10.13140/rg.2.1.3041.0324|year=2015|last1=Tian|first1=Kun|author2=Peichao Gao}}</ref>).
* [https://www.researchgate.net/publication/297736433_RA_calculator_Software_for_calculating_the_ratio_of_areas_RA_in_a_rank-size_plot RA calculator]: Software for calculating the ratio of areas (RA) in a rank-size plot (also see <ref name=":0" />).
* [https://github.com/ChrisdeRijke/HeadTailBreaksCalculator HT 2.0 calculator]: An excel sheet calculator which calculates both head/tail breaks 1.0 and head/tail breaks 2.0 with a version for smaller datasets and a version for very large (binned) datasets.
*'''[https://cran.r-project.org/package=classInt classInt]''': [[R (programming language)|'''R''']] package that implements several  methods for choosing univariate class intervals for mapping or other graphic purposes also includes head/tail breaks map classification.
*[https://github.com/CentroGeo/natural-cities/blob/master/naturalcities/natural_cities.py Natural cities python script]: For generating natural cities using open source python packages
*[https://github.com/ZhengRen91/NC_Gen/blob/main/NC_Gen.py Natural cities python script2]: For generating natural cities from input point data using open source python packages
